claim: eIF4A is a DEAD-box RNA-dependent ATPase thought to unwind RNA secondary structure in the 5'-untranslated regions (UTRs) of mRNAs to promote their recruitment to the eukaryotic translation pre-initiation complex (PIC).
source: eIF4A is a DEAD-box RNA-dependent ATPase thought to unwind RNA secondary structure in the 5'-untranslated regions (UTRs) of mRNAs to promote their recruitment to the eukaryotic translation pre-initiation complex (PIC).
evidence: This is a statement of the prevailing model in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: eIF4A's ATPase activity is markedly stimulated in the presence of the PIC, independently of eIF4E•eIF4G.
source: We show that eIF4A's ATPase activity is markedly stimulated in the presence of the PIC, independently of eIF4E•eIF4G, but dependent on subunits i and g of the heteromeric eIF3 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2, where ATPase activity was measured in various conditions.

claim: eIF4A's ATPase activity stimulation by the PIC is dependent on subunits i and g of the heteromeric eIF3 complex.
source: We show that eIF4A's ATPase activity is markedly stimulated in the presence of the PIC, independently of eIF4E•eIF4G, but dependent on subunits i and g of the heteromeric eIF3 complex.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C and 2D showing that removal of eIF3 subunits 3g and 3i abrogates ATPase stimulation.

claim: eIF4A accelerated the rate of recruitment of all mRNAs tested, regardless of their degree of structural complexity.
source: Surprisingly, eIF4A accelerated the rate of recruitment of all mRNAs tested, regardless of their degree of structural complexity.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 3, where recruitment rates were measured for various mRNAs with different structural complexities.

claim: Structures in the 5'-UTR and 3' of the start codon synergistically inhibit mRNA recruitment in a manner relieved by eIF4A.
source: Structures in the 5'-UTR and 3' of the start codon synergistically inhibit mRNA recruitment in a manner relieved by eIF4A, indicating that the factor does not act solely to melt hairpins in 5'-UTRs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 comparing mRNAs with structures in different locations.

claim: eIF4A functionally interacts with the PIC.
source: Our findings that eIF4A functionally interacts with the PIC and plays important roles beyond unwinding 5'-UTR structure is consistent with a recent proposal that eIF4A modulates the conformation of the 40S ribosomal subunit to promote mRNA recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by the ATPase stimulation data in Figure 2 and is consistent with a cited proposal.

claim: eIF4A plays important roles beyond unwinding 5'-UTR structure.
source: Our findings that eIF4A functionally interacts with the PIC and plays important roles beyond unwinding 5'-UTR structure is consistent with a recent proposal that eIF4A modulates the conformation of the 40S ribosomal subunit to promote mRNA recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by data showing eIF4A accelerates recruitment of unstructured mRNAs (Figures 1 and 3).

claim: The 40S subunit of the ribosome binds eIF1, eIF1A, eIF2, GTP, Met-tRNAi, eIF3, and eIF5 to assemble the 43S PIC.
source: The process begins when the small (40S) subunit of the ribosome binds eIF1, eIF1A, eIF2, GTP, Met-tRNAi, eIF3, and eIF5, to assemble the 43S PIC (Dever et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by the citation to Dever et al., 2016.

claim: eIF1 and eIF1A bind near the P and A sites of the 40S subunit, respectively.
source: eIF1 and eIF1A bind near the P and A sites of the 40S subunit, respectively, and promote loading of the ternary complex (TC) comprising eIF2, GTP, and Met-tRNAi.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field about the binding locations of these factors.

claim: eIF1 and eIF1A promote loading of the ternary complex comprising eIF2, GTP, and Met-tRNAi.
source: eIF1 and eIF1A bind near the P and A sites of the 40S subunit, respectively, and promote loading of the ternary complex (TC) comprising eIF2, GTP, and Met-tRNAi.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of these factors.

claim: eIF5 is the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for eIF2 and stimulates GTP hydrolysis.
source: eIF5 is the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for eIF2 and stimulates GTP hydrolysis (Das et al., 1997, 2001; Paulin et al., 2001); however, irreversible release of the inorganic phosphate is inhibited at this stage of the pathway (Algire et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Irreversible release of the inorganic phosphate is inhibited at the stage of 43S PIC formation.
source: eIF5 is the GTPase-activating protein (GAP) for eIF2 and stimulates GTP hydrolysis (Das et al., 1997, 2001; Paulin et al., 2001); however, irreversible release of the inorganic phosphate is inhibited at this stage of the pathway (Algire et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Algire et al., 2005.

claim: The heteromultimeric factor eIF3 has multiple interactions with the PIC and is involved in nearly every step of translation initiation.
source: The heteromultimeric factor eIF3 has multiple interactions with the PIC and is involved in nearly every step of translation initiation (Aitken and Lorsch, 2012; Valásek, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: The 43S PIC is assembled in an 'open' conformation.
source: The 43S PIC is assembled in an 'open' conformation (Fekete et al., 2007; Llácer et al., 2015; Maag et al., 2005, 2006; Passmore et al., 2007; Pestova et al., 1998a) that can bind an mRNA in a process called mRNA recruitment.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous structural and biochemical studies.

claim: eIF3 and a set of mRNA recruitment factors – eIF4A, eIF4E, eIF4G, and eIF4B – facilitate mRNA recruitment.
source: eIF3 and a set of mRNA recruitment factors – eIF4A, eIF4E, eIF4G, and eIF4B – facilitate this step (Mitchell et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mitchell et al., 2011.

claim: After initial mRNA loading, the PIC remains in an open conformation and scans the 5'-untranslated region (UTR) of the mRNA for the start codon, usually an AUG.
source: After initial mRNA loading, the PIC remains in an open conformation and scans the 5'- untranslated region (UTR) of the mRNA for the start codon, usually an AUG (Hinnebusch, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation to a review.

claim: Recognition of the start codon by the Met-tRNAi triggers eviction of eIF1.
source: Recognition of the start codon by the Met-tRNAi triggers a series of key steps – eviction of eIF1, movement of the C-terminal tail of eIF1A out of the P site, and subsequent release of the previously-hydrolyzed inorganic phosphate by eIF2 – ultimately shifting the PIC from an 'open' to a 'closed' conformation (Dever et al., 2016; Hussain et al., 2014; Llácer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Recognition of the start codon by the Met-tRNAi triggers movement of the C-terminal tail of eIF1A out of the P site.
source: Recognition of the start codon by the Met-tRNAi triggers a series of key steps – eviction of eIF1, movement of the C-terminal tail of eIF1A out of the P site, and subsequent release of the previously-hydrolyzed inorganic phosphate by eIF2 – ultimately shifting the PIC from an 'open' to a 'closed' conformation (Dever et al., 2016; Hussain et al., 2014; Llácer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Recognition of the start codon by the Met-tRNAi triggers release of the previously-hydrolyzed inorganic phosphate by eIF2.
source: Recognition of the start codon by the Met-tRNAi triggers a series of key steps – eviction of eIF1, movement of the C-terminal tail of eIF1A out of the P site, and subsequent release of the previously-hydrolyzed inorganic phosphate by eIF2 – ultimately shifting the PIC from an 'open' to a 'closed' conformation (Dever et al., 2016; Hussain et al., 2014; Llácer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Start codon recognition shifts the PIC from an 'open' to a 'closed' conformation.
source: Recognition of the start codon by the Met-tRNAi triggers a series of key steps – eviction of eIF1, movement of the C-terminal tail of eIF1A out of the P site, and subsequent release of the previously-hydrolyzed inorganic phosphate by eIF2 – ultimately shifting the PIC from an 'open' to a 'closed' conformation (Dever et al., 2016; Hussain et al., 2014; Llácer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The 48S PIC is committed to the selected start codon.
source: The 48S PIC thus formed is committed to the selected start codon and joining with the large (60S) subunit of the ribosome to form the final 80S initiation complex (Acker et al., 2009; Dever et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The individual absence of eIF4A, eIF4B, eIF3, or the eIF4G•eIF4E complex greatly reduces the extent, the rate or both of mRNA recruitment to the PIC in a S. cerevisiae in vitro reconstituted translation initiation system.
source: We demonstrated that the individual absence of eIF4A, eIF4B, eIF3, or the eIF4G•eIF4E complex greatly reduces the extent, the rate or both of mRNA recruitment to the PIC in a S. cerevisiae in vitro reconstituted translation initiation system (Mitchell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: eIF3 binds on the solvent side of the 40S subunit.
source: Structural and biochemical work indicates that eIF3 binds on the solvent side of the 40S subunit but its five core subunits have multiple interactions with other components of the PIC including distinct interactions with the mRNA near the entry and exit channels of the ribosome (Aitken et al., 2016; Llácer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: The five core subunits of eIF3 have multiple interactions with other components of the PIC including distinct interactions with the mRNA near the entry and exit channels of the ribosome.
source: Structural and biochemical work indicates that eIF3 binds on the solvent side of the 40S subunit but its five core subunits have multiple interactions with other components of the PIC including distinct interactions with the mRNA near the entry and exit channels of the ribosome (Aitken et al., 2016; Llácer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Yeast eIF4B binds directly to the 40S ribosomal subunit.
source: Also, yeast eIF4B binds directly to the 40S ribosomal subunit, modulates the conformation of the ribosome near the mRNA entry channel (Walker et al., 2013), and has a functional interaction with eIF4A (Andreou and Klostermeier, 2014; Harms et al., 2014; Park et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Yeast eIF4B modulates the conformation of the ribosome near the mRNA entry channel.
source: Also, yeast eIF4B binds directly to the 40S ribosomal subunit, modulates the conformation of the ribosome near the mRNA entry channel (Walker et al., 2013), and has a functional interaction with eIF4A (Andreou and Klostermeier, 2014; Harms et al., 2014; Park et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Walker et al., 2013.

claim: Yeast eIF4B has a functional interaction with eIF4A.
source: Also, yeast eIF4B binds directly to the 40S ribosomal subunit, modulates the conformation of the ribosome near the mRNA entry channel (Walker et al., 2013), and has a functional interaction with eIF4A (Andreou and Klostermeier, 2014; Harms et al., 2014; Park et al., 2013; Walker et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: eIF4A has not been shown to bind stably to the PIC.
source: In contrast, eIF4A has not been shown to bind stably to the PIC but forms a heterotrimeric complex with eIF4G and eIF4E (eIF4A•4G•4E), collectively referred to as eIF4F, which interacts with the mRNA.
evidence: This is a statement about the lack of evidence for stable binding in previous studies.

claim: eIF4A forms a heterotrimeric complex with eIF4G and eIF4E (eIF4A•4G•4E), collectively referred to as eIF4F.
source: In contrast, eIF4A has not been shown to bind stably to the PIC but forms a heterotrimeric complex with eIF4G and eIF4E (eIF4A•4G•4E), collectively referred to as eIF4F, which interacts with the mRNA.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the eIF4F complex.

claim: Hairpin structures in the 5'-UTR are generally inhibitory to translation initiation.
source: Hairpin structures in the 5'-UTR are generally inhibitory to translation initiation and the prevailing model of mRNA recruitment suggests that eIF4A – localized to the 5'-end via the eIF4G–eIF4E–5'-m7G-cap chain of interactions – unwinds these hairpins to allow PIC attachment (Merrick, 2015; Pelletier and Sonenberg, 1985; Ray et al., 1985; Svitkin et al., 2001; Yoder-Hill et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: The prevailing model of mRNA recruitment suggests that eIF4A – localized to the 5'-end via the eIF4G–eIF4E–5'-m7G-cap chain of interactions – unwinds hairpins in the 5'-UTR to allow PIC attachment.
source: Hairpin structures in the 5'-UTR are generally inhibitory to translation initiation and the prevailing model of mRNA recruitment suggests that eIF4A – localized to the 5'-end via the eIF4G–eIF4E–5'-m7G-cap chain of interactions – unwinds these hairpins to allow PIC attachment (Merrick, 2015; Pelletier and Sonenberg, 1985; Ray et al., 1985; Svitkin et al., 2001; Yoder-Hill et al., 1993).
evidence: This is the prevailing model in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: eIF4A is a DEAD-box RNA-dependent ATPase thought to act as an RNA helicase.
source: eIF4A is a DEAD-box RNA-dependent ATPase thought to act as an RNA helicase (Andreou and Klostermeier, 2013; Linder et al., 1989; Schreier et al., 1977).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: eIF4A cooperatively binds RNA and ATP with no apparent RNA sequence specificity.
source: It cooperatively binds RNA and ATP with no apparent RNA sequence specificity, although, recent ribosome profiling experiments suggested that eIF4A may have a preference for binding polypurine sequences in vivo (Iwasaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge with a caveat from a recent study cited.

claim: Recent ribosome profiling experiments suggested that eIF4A may have a preference for binding polypurine sequences in vivo.
source: It cooperatively binds RNA and ATP with no apparent RNA sequence specificity, although, recent ribosome profiling experiments suggested that eIF4A may have a preference for binding polypurine sequences in vivo (Iwasaki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Iwasaki et al., 2016.

claim: eIF4A is thought to disrupt structures by local strand separation, possibly by bending the RNA duplex.
source: eIF4A is thought to disrupt structures by local strand separation, possibly by bending the RNA duplex (Henn et al., 2012; Linder and Jankowsky, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: ATP hydrolysis to ADP causes a decrease in affinity of eIF4A for RNA, which may allow recycling of the factor.
source: Intermediate states of the catalytic cycle may have higher affinities for RNA; however, ATP hydrolysis to ADP causes a decrease in affinity of eIF4A for RNA, which may allow recycling of the factor (Andreou and Klostermeier, 2013; Jankowsky, 2011; Liu et al., 2008; Lorsch and Herschlag, 1998a; Lorsch and Herschlag, 1998b; Pause et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: Both yeast and mammalian eIF4A are able to disrupt short RNA duplexes in vitro.
source: Several studies demonstrated that both yeast and mammalian eIF4A are able to disrupt short RNA duplexes in vitro (Rajagopal et al., 2012; Ray et al., 1985; Rogers et al., 1999) and more recent work suggests that mammalian eIF4A can unwind a large hairpin when the RNA is stretched between two tethers (García-García et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous experimental work.

claim: Mammalian eIF4A can unwind a large hairpin when the RNA is stretched between two tethers.
source: Several studies demonstrated that both yeast and mammalian eIF4A are able to disrupt short RNA duplexes in vitro (Rajagopal et al., 2012; Ray et al., 1985; Rogers et al., 1999) and more recent work suggests that mammalian eIF4A can unwind a large hairpin when the RNA is stretched between two tethers (García-García et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to García-García et al., 2015.

claim: Sensitivity to inhibition of translation by a dominant negative mutant of mammalian eIF4A is correlated with the degree of secondary structure in the 5'-UTR.
source: Also, sensitivity to inhibition of translation by a dominant negative mutant of mammalian eIF4A is correlated with the degree of secondary structure in the 5'-UTR, supporting a role for eIF4A in removing structures from the 5'-end of mRNAs (Svitkin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Svitkin et al., 2001.

claim: eIF4A is a slow helicase when unwinding stable duplexes in vitro.
source: Nonetheless, eIF4A is a slow helicase when unwinding stable duplexes in vitro (García-García et al., 2015; Lorsch and Herschlag, 1998b; Rajagopal et al., 2012; Rogers et al., 1999) and it is unclear whether it could support in vivo rates of translation initiation in the range of 10 min−1 (Palmiter, 1975; Shah et al., 2013; Siwiak and Zielenkiewicz, 2010) if this is its function.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: In vivo rates of translation initiation are in the range of 10 min−1.
source: Nonetheless, eIF4A is a slow helicase when unwinding stable duplexes in vitro (García-García et al., 2015; Lorsch and Herschlag, 1998b; Rajagopal et al., 2012; Rogers et al., 1999) and it is unclear whether it could support in vivo rates of translation initiation in the range of 10 min−1 (Palmiter, 1975; Shah et al., 2013; Siwiak and Zielenkiewicz, 2010) if this is its function.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Translation of mRNAs with 5'-UTRs possessing high degrees of structure tend to be specifically dependent on Ded1.
source: A study in yeast employing ribosome profiling to compare the in vivo effects of inactivating eIF4A versus Ded1 – a considerably more robust DEAD-box RNA helicase – demonstrated that translation of mRNAs with 5'-UTRs possessing high degrees of structure tend to be specifically dependent on Ded1, but relatively few mRNAs are similarly hyper-dependent on eIF4A, despite comparable requirements for the two helicases in maintaining global translation initiation.
evidence: This is supported by description of a previous study, though the specific citation is not provided in this sentence.

claim: Relatively few mRNAs are hyper-dependent on eIF4A, despite comparable requirements for eIF4A and Ded1 in maintaining global translation initiation.
source: A study in yeast employing ribosome profiling to compare the in vivo effects of inactivating eIF4A versus Ded1 – a considerably more robust DEAD-box RNA helicase – demonstrated that translation of mRNAs with 5'-UTRs possessing high degrees of structure tend to be specifically dependent on Ded1, but relatively few mRNAs are similarly hyper-dependent on eIF4A, despite comparable requirements for the two helicases in maintaining global translation initiation.
evidence: This is supported by description of a previous study.

claim: Yeast eIF4A is either ineffective or dispensable in the presence of Ded1 in resolving stable, local secondary structures in the 5'-UTR.
source: Consistent with this, analysis of reporter mRNAs harboring inhibitory hairpin structures indicated that yeast eIF4A is either ineffective or dispensable in the presence of Ded1 in resolving stable, local secondary structures in the 5'-UTR (Sen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sen et al., 2015.

claim: Minor decreases in the normally high cellular levels of yeast eIF4A resulted in depressed global rates of translation.
source: In a separate study, minor decreases in the normally high cellular levels of yeast eIF4A also resulted in depressed global rates of translation (Firczuk et al., 2013), providing additional evidence that eIF4A may be important for translation of all mRNAs and must be present in excess of other components of the translational apparatus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Firczuk et al., 2013.

claim: eIF4A has been shown to promote translation of an mRNA possessing a short (8 nucleotide (nt)) 5'-UTR.
source: Consistent with the idea that it acts generally rather than by disrupting specific secondary structures in 5'-UTRs, eIF4A has been shown to promote translation of an mRNA possessing a short (8 nucleotide (nt)) 5'-UTR (Blum et al., 1992) and a viral mRNA with a low degree of structure in its 5'-UTR (Altmann et al., 1990), and to stimulate 48S PIC formation on mRNAs with little secondary structure in their 5'-UTRs (Pestova and Kolupaeva, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Blum et al., 1992.

claim: eIF4A has been shown to promote translation of a viral mRNA with a low degree of structure in its 5'-UTR.
source: Consistent with the idea that it acts generally rather than by disrupting specific secondary structures in 5'-UTRs, eIF4A has been shown to promote translation of an mRNA possessing a short (8 nucleotide (nt)) 5'-UTR (Blum et al., 1992) and a viral mRNA with a low degree of structure in its 5'-UTR (Altmann et al., 1990), and to stimulate 48S PIC formation on mRNAs with little secondary structure in their 5'-UTRs (Pestova and Kolupaeva, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Altmann et al., 1990.

claim: eIF4A stimulates 48S PIC formation on mRNAs with little secondary structure in their 5'-UTRs.
source: Consistent with the idea that it acts generally rather than by disrupting specific secondary structures in 5'-UTRs, eIF4A has been shown to promote translation of an mRNA possessing a short (8 nucleotide (nt)) 5'-UTR (Blum et al., 1992) and a viral mRNA with a low degree of structure in its 5'-UTR (Altmann et al., 1990), and to stimulate 48S PIC formation on mRNAs with little secondary structure in their 5'-UTRs (Pestova and Kolupaeva, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Pestova and Kolupaeva, 2002.

claim: Mammalian eIF4A enhances the affinity of mammalian PICs for both a natural and an unstructured model mRNA.
source: Recent experiments using a fluorescence-based equilibrium binding assay indicated that eIF4A enhances the affinity of mammalian PICs for both a natural and an unstructured model mRNA, although ATP hydrolysis was only required for this effect with the natural mRNA (Sokabe and Fraser, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sokabe and Fraser, 2017.

claim: ATP hydrolysis by mammalian eIF4A was only required for enhancement of PIC affinity for mRNA with the natural mRNA but not the unstructured model mRNA.
source: Recent experiments using a fluorescence-based equilibrium binding assay indicated that eIF4A enhances the affinity of mammalian PICs for both a natural and an unstructured model mRNA, although ATP hydrolysis was only required for this effect with the natural mRNA (Sokabe and Fraser, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sokabe and Fraser, 2017.

claim: In the presence of saturating ATP, the rate of recruitment of RPL41A was 0.74 ± 0.01 min−1 with an endpoint in excess of 90%.
source: In the presence of saturating ATP, the rate of recruitment of RPL41A was 0.74 ± 0.01 min−1 with an endpoint in excess of 90%.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: In the presence of ADP, and in reactions lacking either nucleotide or eIF4A, less than 20% of RPL41A mRNA was recruited after 6 hr.
source: In contrast, in the presence of ADP, and in reactions lacking either nucleotide or eIF4A, less than 20% of RPL41A mRNA was recruited after 6 hr, indicating a dramatically lower rate that could not be measured accurately due to the low reaction endpoint (Figure 1A,C).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,C.

claim: The CAA 50-mer was recruited in the absence of eIF4A and ATP at rates of about 0.90 min−1, reaching endpoints around 80%.
source: The CAA 50-mer was recruited in the absence of eIF4A and ATP at rates of about 0.90 min−1, likely due to lack of significant structure, reaching endpoints around 80%.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: The addition of eIF4A and ATP stimulated recruitment of the CAA 50-mer to a rate of at least 4.0 ± 0.6 min−1 and yielded an endpoint of 90%.
source: Surprisingly, the addition of eIF4A and ATP stimulated recruitment of the CAA 50-mer to a rate that could not be measured accurately by manually quenching the reaction; however, we estimate that the increase in rate was at least 4-fold (4.0 ± 0.6 min−1) and yielded an endpoint of 90% (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C.

claim: Neither ADPCP nor ADPNP supported stimulation of the recruitment of either RPL41A or CAA 50-mer mRNA by eIF4A.
source: Neither ADPCP nor ADPNP supported stimulation of the recruitment of either mRNA by eIF4A, producing rates that were comparable to the observed rates measured in the absence of nucleotide or eIF4A (Figure 1; compare grey and blue curves to red and purple).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the presence of ATP-γ-S, recruitment of RPL41A was 39-fold slower than in the presence of ATP.
source: In the presence of ATP-γ-S, recruitment of RPL41A and CAA 50-mer was 39-fold (0.019 ± 0.001 min−1) and nearly 2-fold (2.3 ± 0.2 min−1) slower, respectively, than in the presence of ATP; however, both mRNAs achieved endpoints of approximately 80%, consistent with previous observations that eIF4A is capable of utilizing ATP-γ-S (Peck and Herschlag, 2003).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: In the presence of ATP-γ-S, recruitment of CAA 50-mer was nearly 2-fold slower than in the presence of ATP.
source: In the presence of ATP-γ-S, recruitment of RPL41A and CAA 50-mer was 39-fold (0.019 ± 0.001 min−1) and nearly 2-fold (2.3 ± 0.2 min−1) slower, respectively, than in the presence of ATP; however, both mRNAs achieved endpoints of approximately 80%, consistent with previous observations that eIF4A is capable of utilizing ATP-γ-S (Peck and Herschlag, 2003).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: eIF4A is capable of utilizing ATP-γ-S.
source: In the presence of ATP-γ-S, recruitment of RPL41A and CAA 50-mer was 39-fold (0.019 ± 0.001 min−1) and nearly 2-fold (2.3 ± 0.2 min−1) slower, respectively, than in the presence of ATP; however, both mRNAs achieved endpoints of approximately 80%, consistent with previous observations that eIF4A is capable of utilizing ATP-γ-S (Peck and Herschlag, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Peck and Herschlag, 2003 and the experimental data in Figure 1.

claim: For eIF4A alone (5 µM) the kcat was 0.48 ± 0.04 min−1.
source: For eIF4A alone (5 µM) the kcat was 0.48 ± 0.04 min−1 (Figure 2A), comparable to a previously reported value of 0.20 ± 0.05 min−1 (Rajagopal et al., 2012).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The addition of co-purified full length eIF4G1 and eIF4E (eIF4G•4E) to eIF4A resulted in a 6.5-fold increase in the kcat.
source: Also, congruent with previous findings (Hilbert et al., 2011; Oberer et al., 2005; Rajagopal et al., 2012), the addition of co-purified full length eIF4G1 and eIF4E (eIF4G•4E) to eIF4A, forming the eIF4A•4G•4E heterotrimer, resulted in a 6.5-fold increase in the kcat (Figure 2A, open squares vs. Figure 2B, closed squares).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and 2B, and is consistent with previous findings cited.

claim: Addition of saturating mRNA increased the ATPase activity of eIF4A alone by only 2-fold in the absence of eIF4G•4E.
source: Whereas addition of saturating mRNA increased the ATPase activity of eIF4A alone by only 2-fold in the absence of eIF4G•4E (Figure 2A), a larger (15-fold) increase in kcat occurred in the presence of eIF4G•4E (Figure 2B, closed squares).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Addition of saturating mRNA to eIF4A in the presence of eIF4G•4E resulted in a 15-fold increase in kcat.
source: Whereas addition of saturating mRNA increased the ATPase activity of eIF4A alone by only 2-fold in the absence of eIF4G•4E (Figure 2A), a larger (15-fold) increase in kcat occurred in the presence of eIF4G•4E (Figure 2B, closed squares).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Addition of the PIC to eIF4A•4G•4E in the absence of mRNA increased the kcat 24-fold over the value in the absence of the PIC.
source: Addition of the PIC to eIF4A•4G•4E in the absence of mRNA increased the kcat 24-fold over the value in the absence of the PIC (Figure 2B; compare closed circles and closed squares, respectively, at 0 µM mRNA).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: At saturating concentrations of mRNA, the PIC components enhanced the kcat for ATP hydrolysis by eIF4A•4G•4E by 3.4-fold.
source: However, at saturating concentrations of mRNA, the PIC components still enhanced the kcat for ATP hydrolysis by eIF4A•4G•4E by 3.4-fold (Figure 2B, compare closed circles to closed squares), indicating that there is an enhancement of ATPase activity not due to non-specific stimulation by RNA but instead caused by one or more components of the PIC.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Leaving out 40S subunits from the PIC components resulted in a 2-fold lower kcat at saturating mRNA compared to the value observed in the presence of a Complete PIC.
source: Leaving out 40S subunits from the PIC components resulted in a 2-fold lower kcat at saturating mRNA compared to the value observed in the presence of a Complete PIC (Figure 2B; compare closed and open circles).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The PIC confers an ~6 fold increase in kcat for eIF4A in the absence of eIF4G•4E.
source: As described below, it is noteworthy that the PIC confers an ~6 fold increase in kcat for eIF4A in the absence of eIF4G•4E, which is comparable to the ~4 fold increase conferred by eIF4G•4E itself (Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D; compare '4A' to 'Complete PIC – eIF4G•4E' and '4A' to '4A•4G•4E').
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Replacing capped RPL41A mRNA with uncapped mRNA yielded similar ATPase results.
source: Replacing capped RPL41A mRNA with uncapped mRNA yielded similar results (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the 5'-cap is not critical for the observed stimulation by the PIC or mRNA.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The 5'-cap is not critical for the observed stimulation of eIF4A ATPase by the PIC or mRNA.
source: Replacing capped RPL41A mRNA with uncapped mRNA yielded similar results (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), indicating that the 5'-cap is not critical for the observed stimulation by the PIC or mRNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar results with capped and uncapped mRNA.

claim: The kcat for eIF4A•4G•4E was 2.4 ± 0.1 min−1.
source: The kcat for eIF4A•4G•4E was 2.4 ± 0.1 min−1 and adding the 40S subunit and TC (comprising eIF2, GDPNP, and Met-tRNAi) – which alone are not sufficient to form the PIC – did not have any additional effect (Figure 2C, compare,'4A•4G•4E' and 'TC, 40S, 4A•4G•4E').
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adding the 40S subunit and TC to eIF4A•4G•4E did not have any additional effect on kcat.
source: The kcat for eIF4A•4G•4E was 2.4 ± 0.1 min−1 and adding the 40S subunit and TC (comprising eIF2, GDPNP, and Met-tRNAi) – which alone are not sufficient to form the PIC – did not have any additional effect (Figure 2C, compare,'4A•4G•4E' and 'TC, 40S, 4A•4G•4E').
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Adding the Complete PIC increased the kcat by 3.4-fold to 8.2 ± 0.3 min−1.
source: However, as already noted in Figure 2B, adding the Complete PIC increased the kcat by 3.4-fold to 8.2 ± 0.3 min−1 (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, compare,'4A•4G•4E' and 'Complete PIC').
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Omission of eIF4A from an otherwise Complete PIC resulted in a ≥ 67 fold decrease in the rate of ATPase as compared to the Complete PIC.
source: Omission of eIF4A from an otherwise Complete PIC resulted in a ≥ 67 fold decrease in the rate of ATPase as compared to the Complete PIC (to the limit of detection of the assay), ruling out any significant ATPase contamination in any of the PIC components (Figure 2C, '−4A').
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Leaving out eIF2 decreased the kcat by ~2 fold.
source: Similarly, leaving out eIF2 decreased the kcat by ~2 fold (Figure 2C; compare solid red 'Complete PIC' to cross-hatched, light red '−40S' and '−2' bars), indicating that each of these core components of the PIC is needed for full stimulation, but suggesting that other components of the system can still provide some modest stimulation on their own.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Omitting eIF3 decreased ATPase stimulation by 2.5-fold.
source: Omitting eIF3, which binds tightly to the 43S PIC (composed of eIFs 1, 1A, 3, 5, eIF2·GDPNP·Met-tRNAi, and the 40S subunit,) and contacts both the 40S subunit and multiple factors, decreased ATPase stimulation by 2.5-fold (Figure 2C, compare solid red 'Complete PIC' bars to cross-hatched, light red '−3' bar).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The combined absences of 40S subunits and eIF3 resulted in a 2.7-fold decrease in kcat as compared to the Complete PIC.
source: The combined absences of 40S subunits and eIF3 resulted in a 2.7-fold decrease in kcat as compared to the Complete PIC (Figure 2C; '−2,–40S', '−3,–40S'), close to the full 3.4-fold activation, suggesting that eIF3 bound to a 43S PIC is the functional unit of activation.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: eIF3 bound to a 43S PIC is the functional unit of activation for eIF4A ATPase.
source: The combined absences of 40S subunits and eIF3 resulted in a 2.7-fold decrease in kcat as compared to the Complete PIC (Figure 2C; '−2,–40S', '−3,–40S'), close to the full 3.4-fold activation, suggesting that eIF3 bound to a 43S PIC is the functional unit of activation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that combined absence of 40S and eIF3 accounts for most of the activation effect.

claim: eIF3 by itself was not sufficient to significantly increase the kcat of eIF4A•4G•4E.
source: Consistent with this conclusion, eIF3 by itself was not sufficient to significantly increase the kcat of eIF4A•4G•4E (Figure 2C, compare 'eIF4A•4G•4E', '3, 4A•4G•4E' and 'Complete PIC').
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Leaving out eIF4B or eIF5 had no effect on the stimulation of the ATPase activity of eIF4A•4G•4E.
source: In contrast to the core 43S PIC components and eIF3, leaving out eIF4B or eIF5 had no effect on the stimulation of the ATPase activity of eIF4A•4G•4E.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: S. cerevisiae eIF3 is comprised of 5 core subunits.
source: S. cerevisiae eIF3 is comprised of 5 core subunits and is involved in numerous steps of translation initiation, including mRNA recruitment.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast eIF3.

claim: Yeast eIF3 is essential for mRNA recruitment both in vitro and in vivo.
source: Previous studies showed that yeast eIF3 is essential for mRNA recruitment both in vitro (Mitchell et al., 2010) and in vivo (Jivotovskaya et al., 2006), and that it stabilizes TC binding and promotes PIC interactions with the mRNA at both the mRNA entry and exit channels of the 40S subunit (Aitken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: eIF3 stabilizes TC binding and promotes PIC interactions with the mRNA at both the mRNA entry and exit channels of the 40S subunit.
source: Previous studies showed that yeast eIF3 is essential for mRNA recruitment both in vitro (Mitchell et al., 2010) and in vivo (Jivotovskaya et al., 2006), and that it stabilizes TC binding and promotes PIC interactions with the mRNA at both the mRNA entry and exit channels of the 40S subunit (Aitken et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aitken et al., 2016.

claim: The eIF3 subunits 3g and 3i have been implicated in scanning and AUG recognition in vivo.
source: In particular, the eIF3 subunits 3g and 3i have been implicated in scanning and AUG recognition in vivo (Cuchalová et al., 2010) and are required for recruitment of RPL41A mRNA in vitro (Aitken et al., 2016; Valásek, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: eIF3 subunits 3g and 3i are required for recruitment of RPL41A mRNA in vitro.
source: In particular, the eIF3 subunits 3g and 3i have been implicated in scanning and AUG recognition in vivo (Cuchalová et al., 2010) and are required for recruitment of RPL41A mRNA in vitro (Aitken et al., 2016; Valásek, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: eIF3 subunits 3g and 3i are thought to be located near the path of the mRNA on the ribosome, at either the solvent or intersubunit face of the 40S subunit.
source: Both subunits are thought to be located near the path of the mRNA on the ribosome, at either the solvent or intersubunit face of the 40S subunit, and may undergo large alterations in position during initiation (Aylett et al., 2015; des Georges et al., 2015; Llácer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: eIF3 subunits 3g and 3i may undergo large alterations in position during initiation.
source: Both subunits are thought to be located near the path of the mRNA on the ribosome, at either the solvent or intersubunit face of the 40S subunit, and may undergo large alterations in position during initiation (Aylett et al., 2015; des Georges et al., 2015; Llácer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: In the presence of PICs formed with the heterotrimer of eIF3 subunits 3a, 3b, and 3c – but lacking the 3g and 3i subunits – the kcat was 3.9 ± 0.3 min−1.
source: In the presence of PICs formed with the heterotrimer of eIF3 subunits 3a, 3b, and 3c – but lacking the 3g and 3i subunits – the kcat was 3.9 ± 0.3 min−1, which is similar to the rate constant observed in the absence of the entire eIF3 complex (Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, '−3' vs. '−3g, −3i').
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The heterotrimeric eIF3a•3b•3c subcomplex binds to the PIC under experimental conditions.
source: Thus, although the heterotrimeric eIF3a•3b•3 c subcomplex binds to the PIC under our experimental conditions (Aitken et al., 2016) it does not increase the ATPase kcat, indicating an important role for the eIF3i and eIF3g subunits in promoting ATPase activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Aitken et al., 2016.

claim: The heterotrimeric eIF3a•3b•3c subcomplex does not increase the ATPase kcat.
source: Thus, although the heterotrimeric eIF3a•3b•3 c subcomplex binds to the PIC under our experimental conditions (Aitken et al., 2016) it does not increase the ATPase kcat, indicating an important role for the eIF3i and eIF3g subunits in promoting ATPase activity.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data showing similar kcat values with and without the entire eIF3 complex when 3g and 3i are absent.

claim: eIF4A on its own, in the presence of saturating RPL41A mRNA but in the absence of any PIC components or eIF4G•4E, had a kcat of 0.58 ± 0.08 min−1.
source: eIF4A on its own, in the presence of saturating RPL41A mRNA but in the absence of any PIC components or eIF4G•4E, had a kcat of 0.58 ± 0.08 min−1 in these experiments (titrating the concentration of ATP).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Addition of the PIC, without eIF4G•4E, resulted in a 6-fold increase in kcat over eIF4A alone.
source: Addition of the PIC, without eIF4G•4E, resulted in a 6-fold increase in kcat over eIF4A alone (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; '4A' vs. 'Complete PIC −4G•﻿4E').
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The stimulation of eIF4A by the PIC (6-fold) is even greater than the stimulation of eIF4A•4G•4E by the PIC (3.4-fold) and of eIF4A by the eIF4G•4E complex alone (4.0-fold).
source: Remarkably, this stimulation is even greater than the stimulation of eIF4A•4G•4E by the PIC (3.4-fold) and of eIF4A by the eIF4G•4E complex alone (4.0-fold; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: In the presence of the PIC, eIF4G•4E only increases the kcat for eIF4A by 2.3-fold.
source: In fact, in the presence of the PIC, eIF4G•4E only increases the kcat for eIF4A by 2.3-fold (Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D; compare 'Complete PIC' and 'Complete PIC – eIF4G•4E'), ~2 fold less than the effect of eIF4G•4E on eIF4A in isolation.
evidence: This is directly supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 2C,D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Eliminating the 40S subunit, eIF2, eIF3, or the 3g and 3i subunits of eIF3 in the absence of eIF4G•4E abrogated all stimulation of ATPase activity.
source: Eliminating the 40S subunit, eIF2, eIF3, or the 3g and 3i subunits of eIF3 in the absence of eIF4G•4E abrogated all stimulation of ATPase activity, yielding kcat values the same as those observed with eIF4A alone (~0.6 min−1; Figure 2D, compare dark blue bar to light blue cross-hatched bars).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Stimulation of the ATPase activity of eIF4A, in the absence of eIF4G•4E, requires the complete 43S PIC and eIF3, in particular subunits 3i and 3g.
source: These data suggest that stimulation of the ATPase activity of eIF4A, in the absence of eIF4G•4E, requires the complete 43S PIC and eIF3, in particular subunits 3i and 3g.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that removal of these components abrogates stimulation.

claim: Adding the Complete PIC to eIF4A does not reduce the Km for ATP.
source: In contrast to the effect of eIF4G•4E, adding the Complete PIC to eIF4A does not reduce the Km for ATP; and, as might be expected, leaving out the 40S subunits, eIF2 or eIF3 from the PIC does not increase the Km (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Both the PIC components and eIF4G•4E increase eIF4A's kcat for ATP hydrolysis, but only eIF4G•4E reduces the Km for ATP, suggesting different mechanisms of stimulation.
source: Thus, although both the PIC components and eIF4G•4E increase eIF4A's kcat for ATP hydrolysis, only eIF4G•4E reduces the Km for ATP, suggesting different mechanisms of stimulation.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing different effects on Km.

claim: eIF4G acts as a 'soft clamp' to juxtapose the two eIF4A RecA-like domains to enhance ATP binding and catalysis.
source: The effect of eIF4G•4E is consistent with the proposal that eIF4G acts as a 'soft clamp' to juxtapose the two eIF4A RecA-like domains to enhance ATP binding and catalysis (Hilbert et al., 2011; Oberer et al., 2005; Schütz et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: The PIC components act in a manner that enhances the rate-limiting step of ATP hydrolysis.
source: By contrast, the PIC components apparently act in a manner that enhances the rate-limiting step of ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that PIC increases kcat but not Km.

claim: In the absence of eIF4A, less than 10% of RPL41A mRNA was recruited.
source: Less than 10% of RPL41A mRNA was recruited in reactions lacking eIF4A (Figure 3B, RNA 10, red bar), consistent with the low levels of RPL41A recruitment we observed in the absence of ATP (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Recruitment of RPL41A proceeds two orders of magnitude more rapidly in the presence of saturating levels of eIF4A versus in the absence of eIF4A.
source: However, comparison of estimated initial rates (no eIF4A, 0.22 ± 0.07 min−1; saturating eIF4A, 41 ± 1 min−1) of recruitment of RPL41A revealed that recruitment proceeds two orders of magnitude more rapidly in the presence of saturating levels of eIF4A versus in the absence of eIF4A (Figure 3D, RNA 10).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 74 ± 1% of CAA 50-mer mRNA was recruited in the absence of eIF4A.
source: Consistent with our observation that the unstructured CAA 50-mer mRNA is efficiently recruited even in the absence of ATP, we observed 74 ± 1% recruitment of this mRNA in the absence of eIF4A (Figure 3A–B, RNA 1, red bar).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A–B.

claim: The addition of saturating eIF4A increased the extent of recruitment of CAA 50-mer to 87 ± 1%.
source: Nonetheless, the addition of saturating eIF4A increased the extent of recruitment to 87 ± 1% (Figure 3A–B, RNA 1, black bar) consistent with our observation that the addition of ATP and eIF4A slightly elevates the extent of recruitment of this mRNA above the levels observed in the absence of ATP or eIF4A (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A–B.

claim: Saturating eIF4A markedly accelerated the rate of CAA 50-mer recruitment, yielding a kmax of 6.2 ± 1.0 min−1.
source: Beyond this modest stimulation of recruitment extent, saturating eIF4A markedly accelerated the rate of CAA 50-mer recruitment, yielding a kmax of 6.2 ± 1.0 min−1 (Figure 3C, RNA 1).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the absence of eIF4A, neither the cap-proximal nor the cap-distal hairpins significantly influenced the extent of recruitment, achieving endpoints between 70% and 80%.
source: To our surprise, in the absence of eIF4A, neither the cap-proximal nor the cap-distal hairpins significantly influenced the extent of recruitment, achieving endpoints between 70% and 80%, comparable to the unstructured CAA 50-mer and 250-mer RNAs (Figure 3B, RNAs 5–6 vs. 1–4).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The kmax in the presence of eIF4A for both hairpin-containing mRNAs (RNAs 5–6) were ~2 fold lower than the kmax for the CAA 250-mers lacking the hairpin (RNAs 1–4).
source: The kmax in the presence of eIF4A for both hairpin-containing mRNAs (RNAs 5–6) were ~2 fold lower than the kmax for the CAA 250-mers lacking the hairpin (RNAs 1–4) but the kmax values were 2–3-fold higher than the kmax for RPL41A (Figure 3C, RNAs 5–6 vs. 10).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Addition of a cap-proximal or cap-distal hairpin in the 5'-UTR of an otherwise unstructured mRNA confers little or no inhibition of the extent of recruitment and only a modest reduction in the rate, in the presence or absence of eIF4A.
source: Thus, at odds with the expectation that stable structures in the 5'-UTR would impose strong obstacles to mRNA recruitment to the PIC, we found that addition of a cap-proximal or cap-distal hairpin in the 5'-UTR of an otherwise unstructured mRNA confers little or no inhibition of the extent of recruitment and only a modest reduction in the rate, in the presence or absence of eIF4A.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing similar recruitment endpoints and rates for mRNAs with and without hairpins.

claim: In the presence of saturating eIF4A the kmax for RNA 7 was comparable to the kmax values observed with RNAs 2, 3, 5 and 6 and within 2-fold of the kmax values for RNAs 1 and 4.
source: In contrast, in the presence of saturating eIF4A the kmax for RNA 7 was comparable to the kmax values observed with RNAs 2, 3, 5 and 6 and within 2-fold of the kmax values for RNAs 1 and 4.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: eIF4A can efficiently resolve inhibition of mRNA recruitment mediated by RNA sequences on the 3' side of the start codon.
source: These results indicate that eIF4A can efficiently resolve inhibition of mRNA recruitment mediated by RNA sequences on the 3' side of the start codon, which are not predicted to form stable secondary structures with the 5'-UTR (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D) (Zuker, 2003).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing large rate enhancement by eIF4A for RNA 7.

claim: The presence of saturating eIF4A dramatically increased recruitment of mRNAs 8 and 9 to ~80%.
source: Moreover, the presence of saturating eIF4A dramatically increased recruitment of both of these mRNAs to ~80% (Figure 3B, RNAs 8–9, black vs. red bars) and also increased their kmax values by approximately 10-fold (Figure 3D, RNAs 8–9).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3D.

claim: The combined effects of structures in the 5'-UTR and 3' to the AUG (in RNAs 8 and 9) is considerably more than the additive effects of either structural element alone (in RNAs 5–7).
source: Comparing kmax values for RNA 4 to RNAs 5–9 shows that the combined effects of structures in the 5'-UTR and 3' to the AUG (in RNAs 8 and 9) is considerably more than the additive effects of either structural element alone (in RNAs 5–7) (Figure 3C, RNAs 4–9; Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is directly supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Structures in the 5'-UTR and structures 3' to the start codon synergistically inhibit the rate of mRNA recruitment.
source: Because the additive effects of structures in the 5'-UTR (RNAs 5 and 6) and structures 3' to the start codon (RNA 7) would only be ~6 fold (~2-fold X ~ 3 fold), the >30 fold effect observed by combining them indicates that structures in both regions synergistically inhibit the rate of mRNA recruitment.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing greater than additive effects.

claim: eIF4A restores the extent of recruitment of RNAs 8 and 9, albeit at relatively low recruitment rates.
source: The fact that eIF4A restores the extent of recruitment of RNAs 8 and 9 (Figure 3B, RNAs 8–9, black bars), albeit at relatively low recruitment rates, indicates that eIF4A can eventually resolve the synergistic inhibition produced by structures in the 5' and 3' segments of these messenger RNAs.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: eIF4A gives considerably larger rate enhancements for the mRNAs harboring only native RPL41A sequences (RNAs 7 and 10) than those burdened with synthetic hairpins (RNAs 5–6 and 8–9).
source: It is noteworthy, however, that eIF4A gives considerably larger rate enhancements (Figure 3D) for the mRNAs harboring only native RPL41A sequences (RNAs 7 and 10) than those burdened with synthetic hairpins (RNAs 5–6 and 8–9), suggesting that eIF4A is better able to resolve the complex array of relatively less stable structures in RPL41A compared to a highly stable local structure in the 5'-UTR.
evidence: This is directly supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The kmax observed with saturating eIF4A was comparable with or without the 5'-cap for RNAs 1 and 7.
source: As summarized in Figure 4B, the kmax observed with saturating eIF4A was comparable with or without the 5'-cap for RNAs 1 and 7, and was 1.5-fold lower with the cap than without it for RNA 4.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In the absence of eIF4A, the rates of recruitment for uncapped versions of the unstructured model mRNAs 1 and 4 were 3.7- and 2.5-fold higher, respectively, than the rates of the corresponding 5'-capped mRNAs.
source: In contrast, in the absence of eIF4A, the rates of recruitment for uncapped versions of the unstructured model mRNAs 1 and 4 were 3.7- and 2.5-fold higher, respectively, than the rates of the corresponding 5'-capped mRNAs (Figure 4A,B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1, compare 0 µM eIF4A points in the inset graphs).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: RNA 7 was recruited 15-fold faster when uncapped versus capped in the absence of eIF4A.
source: This effect was even more pronounced for RNA 7, containing natural mRNA sequence 3' of the AUG, which was recruited 15-fold faster when uncapped versus capped in the absence of eIF4A.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Even for short mRNAs with low structural complexity, the 5'-cap inhibits recruitment in the absence of eIF4A.
source: Taken together, our data indicate that even for short mRNAs with low structural complexity, the 5'-cap inhibits recruitment in the absence of eIF4A, consistent with our previous observations with a natural mRNA and our proposal that the cap serves, in part, to enforce use of the canonical mRNA recruitment pathway (Mitchell et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing reduced recruitment rates for capped mRNAs in the absence of eIF4A.

claim: Mammalian eIF4G interacts with eIF3, which could serve to bring the eIF4F complex onto the PIC.
source: In addition, in mammals (but not S. cerevisiae) eIF4G interacts with eIF3, which could serve to bring the eIF4F complex onto the PIC (des Georges et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to des Georges et al., 2015.

claim: Mammalian eIF4G binds to the 40S subunit near the eukaryotic expansion segment 6 of the 18S rRNA.
source: Some support for a model in which eIF4F interacts with the PIC to promote mRNA recruitment came from hydroxyl radical footprinting experiments that indicated mammalian eIF4G binds to the 40S subunit near the eukaryotic expansion segment 6 of the 18S rRNA (Yu et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yu et al., 2011.

claim: Mammalian eIF4B interacts with 40S subunit rRNA.
source: Other work has indicated that yeast eIF4B binds to the 40S ribosomal subunit (Walker et al., 2013) and modulates the conformation of the mRNA entry channel, and that mammalian eIF4B interacts with 40S subunit rRNA (Methot et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Methot et al., 1996.

claim: eIF4A is required in reconstituted translation systems for 48S PIC formation.
source: The factor is required in reconstituted translation systems for 48S PIC formation (Benne and Hershey, 1978; Pestova and Kolupaeva, 2002; Schreier and Staehelin, 1973), and in mammalian extracts the eIF4A-dependence of translation of different reporter mRNAs was correlated with their degree of 5'-UTR structure (Svitkin et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Mammalian eIF4A was shown to perform a critical function in 48S PIC formation on β-globin mRNA that could not be executed by other helicases (Dhx29 or Ded1) more effective than eIF4A in resolving stem-loop structures within 5'-UTRs.
source: On the other hand, mammalian eIF4A has also been shown to stimulate initiation in vitro on mRNAs with low degrees of 5'-UTR structure (Blum et al., 1992; Pestova and Kolupaeva, 2002), and it was shown to perform a critical function in 48S PIC formation on β-globin mRNA that could not be executed by other helicases (Dhx29 or Ded1) more effective than eIF4A in resolving stem-loop structures within 5'-UTRs (Abaeva et al., 2011; Pisareva et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Abaeva et al., 2011 and Pisareva et al., 2008.

claim: Mammalian eIF4A is required for full accommodation of the 5'-UTR of β-globin mRNA in the mRNA entry channel of the 40S subunit.
source: Recent results indicate that mammalian eIF4A is required for full accommodation of the 5'-UTR of β-globin mRNA in the mRNA entry channel of the 40S subunit (Sokabe and Fraser, 2017), and other evidence suggests that eIF4A is required to position eIF4E at the 40S entry channel for threading the capped 5'-end of the mRNA into the 40S subunit (Kumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sokabe and Fraser, 2017.

claim: eIF4A is required to position eIF4E at the 40S entry channel for threading the capped 5'-end of the mRNA into the 40S subunit.
source: Recent results indicate that mammalian eIF4A is required for full accommodation of the 5'-UTR of β-globin mRNA in the mRNA entry channel of the 40S subunit (Sokabe and Fraser, 2017), and other evidence suggests that eIF4A is required to position eIF4E at the 40S entry channel for threading the capped 5'-end of the mRNA into the 40S subunit (Kumar et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kumar et al., 2016.

claim: The vast majority of mRNAs display a similar, strong dependence on eIF4A for efficient translation.
source: Ribosome profiling studies in yeast revealed that the vast majority of mRNAs display a similar, strong dependence on eIF4A for efficient translation, whereas mRNAs with long, structured 5'-UTRs generally exhibit a special dependence on the helicase Ded1 in addition to their general requirement for eIF4A (Sen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sen et al., 2015.

claim: mRNAs with long, structured 5'-UTRs generally exhibit a special dependence on the helicase Ded1 in addition to their general requirement for eIF4A.
source: Ribosome profiling studies in yeast revealed that the vast majority of mRNAs display a similar, strong dependence on eIF4A for efficient translation, whereas mRNAs with long, structured 5'-UTRs generally exhibit a special dependence on the helicase Ded1 in addition to their general requirement for eIF4A (Sen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sen et al., 2015.

claim: One function of eIF4A is to modulate the conformation of the 40S ribosomal subunit.
source: Taken together with our observation that the PIC accelerates ATP hydrolysis by eIF4A, one explanation for the ability of eIF4A to stimulate mRNA recruitment regardless of 5'-UTR structure would be that one function of eIF4A is to modulate the conformation of the 40S ribosomal subunit, as recently proposed by Sokabe and Fraser (Sokabe and Fraser, 2017).
evidence: This is proposed as an explanation for the authors' data and is consistent with a recent proposal cited.

claim: ATP hydrolysis by eIF4A might act to open the mRNA entry channel, allowing the PIC to engage with and/or move along the mRNA.
source: For instance, ATP hydrolysis by eIF4A, stimulated at least in part by eIF3 subunits, might act to open the mRNA entry channel, allowing the PIC to engage with and/or move along the mRNA (Figure 5A) – similar to the proposed function of mammalian helicase Dhx29 (Hashem et al., 2013; Pisareva et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative model proposed by the authors based on their data and analogy to another helicase.

claim: eIF4A – which is present in large excess of ribosomes in vivo – binds to an mRNA throughout its length.
source: In the holistic model, eIF4A – which is present in large excess of ribosomes in vivo (Firczuk et al., 2013) – binds to an mRNA throughout its length (Lindqvist et al., 2008) and mediates the relaxation of local structures, helping to expose the 5'-cap.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: eIF4A is not required for 48S PIC assembly with certain internal ribosome entry sites (IRESs), for example that of hepatitis C virus.
source: The fact that eIF4A is not required for 48S PIC assembly with certain internal ribosome entry sites (IRESs), for example that of hepatitis C virus (Pestova et al., 1998b; Spahn et al., 2001), can be explained by proposing that IRES interactions with the 40S subunit evoke a conformational change in the ribosome that enables the initiation region of the mRNA to bind directly into the mRNA binding cleft, bypassing all proposed functions of eIF4A in PIC attachment and scanning (Doudna and Sarnow, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and is used to support the authors' model.
